opus-5.5.text:
When I was assessing Shubho, I didn't really treat "director-level experience" as a checkbox. A title can mean very different things at different companies, so I tried to look past it and ask what the person actually built and how they operated.

A few things mattered to me.

First, did he still have his hands on the technical work? At a big lab, some directors become pure managers: they run meetings, do headcount planning, and are far from the code and the experiments. For an early-stage company like ours, that doesn't work. We need someone who can sit down, look at a training run, understand why the loss curve looks strange, and have an opinion about the infrastructure. With Shubho, it was very clear in our conversations that he still thinks like an engineer. He could go deep on systems details, on GPUs, on what makes large-scale training efficient. That was a big signal.

Second, I looked at whether he had built teams from scratch, not just inherited them. Scaling something from zero to one is a very different skill from maintaining something that already works. I wanted to hear specific stories: who he hired, why, what went wrong, what he would do differently. People who have really done it can tell you about failures in a very concrete way.

Third, honestly, I was looking at judgment and taste. At the director level you've seen a lot of projects succeed and fail, and the question is whether you learned the right lessons. I'd ask him about bets he made, research directions he pushed for or killed, and listen to how he reasoned.

And finally, there's the human side. I'm a young founder, and someone with that much experience could easily come in and be dismissive, or try to run things the way a big company does. I paid close attention to whether he was genuinely excited about building something new and scrappy, and whether we could disagree productively. With Shubho, the conversations felt like two people trying to solve the same problem, not an interview where he was evaluating whether we were serious enough. That mutual respect mattered a lot to me in the end.

r001.rationale: The response mentions experience with projects that succeeded or failed, but does not convey an expectation that many of Shubho’s projects had long delivery timelines.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't assess it the way a traditional founder might, looking at a résumé and checking boxes. I'd just come out of academia, so I had very little experience in corporate hierarchies. What I cared about was whether this person could actually build the thing we were setting out to build, and whether I could learn from him.

Shubho had spent years at Meta in roles where he was responsible for very large infrastructure and research systems, and he'd done it at a level where he wasn't just writing code but deciding what the team should be working on at all. That mattered to me more than the title. A director-level person has to make decisions with incomplete information, manage people who are smarter than them in specific areas, and still ship. Those are exactly the muscles a founding team at a company like Axiom needs, because we're trying to do formal math reasoning at scale, which is both a research problem and a systems problem.

So the way I assessed it was actually through conversation. We'd talk about a technical problem, for example how to structure training on formal proof data, and I'd watch how he reasoned. Did he jump to the answer, or did he ask the right questions first? Did he push back on me when I was wrong? He pushed back a lot, which I liked. I also talked to people who had worked under him. The consistent thing I heard was that he gave people room but held the bar high, and that's hard to fake over years.

I'd also say his experience gave him something I didn't have, which was a sense of how fast things break when you scale from three people to thirty. I've seen that now, and I was glad to have someone who had already lived through it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Shubho’s responsibility for large systems and his management and decision-making experience, but does not convey an expectation that he handled many projects with long delivery timelines.
